title: Know for yourselves
hookLine: to the Kalamas: not by tradition, scripture or logic alone; when you know for yourselves (AN 3.65)

lines: A TOWN THE TEACHERS PASS THROUGH.
WHICH ONE IS TELLING THE TRUTH?
cards: Kesaputta is a town of the Kalama people, and wandering teachers keep passing through. Each one arrives, explains his own teaching beautifully, and then tears down everyone else's. Then the next one does the same.
The Kalamas are worn out. When the Buddha passes through, they put it to him straight: we have doubts, sir. Which of these people is telling the truth?
It sounds like a very modern question: with everyone so sure, how do you know?

teach.h: IT IS FITTING FOR YOU TO DOUBT
teach.b: The Buddha starts by agreeing with them. It's fitting for you to doubt, Kalamas. You doubt where doubt is fitting.
Then the list, paraphrased. Don't go by what's been handed down, or by lineage, or by hearsay. Not by a collection of scriptures.

teach.h: NOT BY TRADITION, SCRIPTURE OR LOGIC ALONE
teach.b: Not by logic, inference, or thinking about reasons, not by a view you've grown fond of after pondering it. Not because the speaker seems capable, and not because you think, this monk is our teacher.
Ten things, and they include his own authority. But the line doesn't stop at don't.

When you know for yourselves that these things are unwholesome, blameworthy, criticized by the wise, and lead to harm and suffering when taken up, abandon them. When you know for yourselves the opposite, take them up.
Then he doesn't lecture. He asks.

teach.h: GREED: FOR WELFARE OR FOR HARM?
teach.b: When greed arises in a person, is it for their welfare or their harm? Harm, sir. Someone overcome by greed kills, steals, goes after another's partner, lies, and gets others to do the same.
Does that lead to harm? Yes, sir. Then hatred, the same questions.
Then delusion. The Kalamas answer every one themselves, from their own lives.
That's the method: not trust me, but look.
A modern note. A line often posted online, believe nothing, no matter where you read it or who said it, is a loose modern paraphrase, not the text.
The real passage is less sweeping and more useful: check what you're told against what actually helps and harms, and against the wise.

how: Buddhist teachers often cite the Kalama Sutta to encourage students to test the teaching in their own practice, while traditional teachers also stress that the passage includes checking against what the wise praise.

o: a wandering teacher who doubted all
a village elder who kept the scriptures
the clan who asked whom to trust

p: every teacher runs down the others
does it lead to harm or welfare?

s: the Kalama Sutta says believe nothing anyone tells you
it says not by tradition, scripture or logic alone; know for yourselves what helps and harms, including what the wise praise.
the list of things not to rely on includes the teacher himself
not because you think, this monk is our teacher.
the Buddha answers the Kalamas with a long lecture
he asks them questions about greed, hatred and delusion, and they answer from their own lives.

games.q: you're a Kalama. teacher after teacher praises his own way and attacks the others. you ask the Buddha whom to trust. what does he say?
o: trust me; I am the awakened one.
doubt is fitting; know for yourselves what leads to harm and what to welfare.
games.why: he praises their doubt, lists ten things not to rely on alone, including himself, and then has them test greed, hatred and delusion against their own experience.

practice: Choose one belief you hold about how to live, small is fine, like I need to stay busy to be worth something, and ask it the Buddha's questions: when I act on this, does it lead to welfare or to harm, for me, for others?
Would the wise people I know praise it, or wince? Don't force an answer; just look honestly at what happens when you act on it, then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Kalama. The clan of Kesaputta who asked the Buddha whom to trust among many teachers, in AN 3.65: not by tradition or logic alone, but by what you find true for yourself. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Kalama: the clan of Kesaputta, to whom AN 3.65 is spoken, so it is often called the Kalama Sutta.

carryVoice: Your line: check it against what helps. Doubt, the Buddha said, can be fitting. Day six hundred fifty-seven, done.
